problem: README says handles are case-insensitive (@Ada, @ada and @ADA are one account), but the column is 'TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE' with default BINARY collation. The UNIQUE constraint only blocks exact-case duplicates, so 'Ada' and 'ada' can both be inserted. The sample (120,000 rows) happens to contain no case collisions, but nothing prevents them, and the 1.2M beta migration was never checked for them. Duplicates mean impersonation and mentions that resolve to the wrong person.
fix: Declare the column 'handle TEXT NOT NULL COLLATE NOCASE UNIQUE' (keeps the owner's typed case for display, enforces uniqueness case-insensitively, and the index serves NOCASE lookups). Before migrating, find collisions with SELECT lower(handle), count(*) FROM account GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1 and resolve them. SQLite NOCASE folds only ASCII, which matches the [A-Za-z0-9_] handle pattern; enforce that pattern in signup too.

problem: 'WHERE handle = :handle COLLATE NOCASE' cannot use the BINARY-collated UNIQUE index, so EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows 'SCAN account USING COVERING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_account_1': a full scan of every account per lookup. At 1.2M accounts and about 300 posts/s with 2 mentions each (about 600 lookups/s), the single writer scans about 720M index entries per second, so posting will fall over at launch. It also returns every matching row but record_mentions uses fetchone(), so with case-variant duplicates the winner is arbitrary.
fix: Fix the column collation (see account.handle) and drop the per-query COLLATE override, so the plan becomes SEARCH account USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_account_1 (handle=?). Add LIMIT 1 or rely on the real uniqueness guarantee.

problem: Same defect as resolve_mention.sql: 'handle = :handle COLLATE NOCASE' does a full covering-index scan of account on every signup attempt, and signups are exactly what is about to be opened up.
fix: Fix the column collation and remove COLLATE NOCASE from the query so it becomes an index SEARCH.

problem: Check-then-insert race: handle_taken is a plain SELECT run before the INSERT, and in Python's sqlite3 the transaction only begins at the INSERT, so 'with con' does not make the check and insert atomic. A second connection can take the handle in between. Because the UNIQUE constraint is case-sensitive, even the loser of the race may not be rejected by the database. Raw sqlite3.IntegrityError can also leak to the caller.
fix: Rely on the database constraint (case-insensitive UNIQUE, see account.handle): just INSERT and translate sqlite3.IntegrityError into ValueError('handle taken'), or use BEGIN IMMEDIATE around check and insert. Validate the handle against [A-Za-z0-9_]{2,30} first, since mentions can only match that pattern.

problem: The plan shows 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY': the query joins every post by every followee and sorts them all by posted_at before applying LIMIT 50. post_by_author (author_id, posted_at) is per-author, so it cannot give a merged order. Cost grows with follows times posts-per-author on every timeline load; accounts following thousands of heavy posters will be slow. posted_at is also stored as a date-like TEXT ('2026-11-09' in the sample), so many posts tie and the order and any pagination are unstable. There is no cursor/keyset condition either.
fix: Order by (posted_at DESC, p.id DESC) with a timestamp that has real resolution, add a keyset predicate for paging, and bound the work: either fan-out-on-write into a per-user timeline table or cap the per-followee window (e.g. only posts newer than a cutoff) before sorting.

problem: 'LIMIT 100' without ORDER BY or any cursor: followers beyond the first 100 cannot be reached, and which 100 appear is not defined. Index follow_by_followee does serve the lookup (SEARCH ... COVERING INDEX), so the problem is semantics, not speed.
fix: Add ORDER BY f.follower_id and a keyset parameter (AND f.follower_id > :after) for paging.

problem: The dedupe set(HANDLE.findall(body)) is case-sensitive, so '@Ada @ada' triggers two lookups (INSERT OR IGNORE hides the second insert). Each handle is resolved with a separate query inside the posting path, and the regex also matches the tail of an email address such as 'a@bob'. The function does not check the connection is inside a transaction, so a failure mid-loop leaves a partial set of mentions.
fix: Lowercase the handles before the set, require a non-word character before '@' in HANDLE, resolve all handles in one query (WHERE handle IN (...)), and run the whole post plus mentions insert in one transaction.

problem: The table has the right keys, but record_mentions inserts positionally ('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO mention VALUES (?, ?)') with no column list, which breaks silently if columns are ever added or reordered. mention_by_account (account_id, post_id) is fine for mentions_of.sql.
fix: Name the columns: INSERT OR IGNORE INTO mention (post_id, account_id) VALUES (?, ?).

problem: The REFERENCES clauses on follow, post and mention are not enforced unless PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON is set on every connection, and nothing in db/ or app/ sets it (with a reader pool, each pooled connection needs it). There is also no CHECK (follower_id <> followee_id), so an account can follow itself. The sample currently has no violations, but nothing stops them.
fix: Execute PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON when each connection is opened and add CHECK (follower_id <> followee_id) to follow.

problem: Index (author_id, posted_at) is used by timeline.sql only for lookups per author; it does not remove the sort. No index serves 'newest posts overall'. post.posted_at and account.joined_at are untyped TEXT with no format check.
fix: Keep it for profile pages, add a CHECK on the timestamp format (or store integer epoch milliseconds), and decide the timeline strategy per db/queries/timeline.sql.

problem: Plan is fine (SEARCH m USING COVERING INDEX mention_by_account, then post by primary key), but LIMIT 50 has no cursor so older mentions are unreachable, and it returns p.body for deleted/blocked authors without any filter.
fix: Add a keyset parameter (AND m.post_id < :before) for paging.
